The programme addresses two main priorities in the region that have been identified during the formulation process – (i) to promote more integrated solutions for climate action that brings benefits across SDGs and for crisis prevention/recovery goals, and (ii) to scale up local partnerships and finance to this end. Through a combination of regional dialogues and technical assistance at the regional level, and innovation grants at the country level, the programme would generate three key outcomes: • Outcome 1: Enhanced knowledge and coordination on climate-security among key stakeholders at the regional level to achieve climate action with co-benefits across the SDGs, and crisis prevention/recovery goals. • Outcome 2: Enhanced access to analysis, tools and strategies at the regional level to support a climate nexus approach to achieving SDGs and prevention/recovery • Outcome 3: Strengthened national and local capacities to effectively integrate climate change considerations into development and crisis prevention/recovery policies and to scale-up climate finance for local innovative solutions with co-benefits across the SDGs Underlying and cutting across these outcomes will be the establishment of SDG-Climate Facility, which will take forward a nexus approach beyond the life-cycle of the project. The programme will focus on the following countries to develop local capacity, deploy integrated solutions and support scale-up of climate financing: Egypt, Iraq, Palestine, Tunisia, Yemen, as well as a response to the Syria crisis in Jordan as a host country of Syrian refugees.

This Annual Report covered the period 1 January 2023- 31st of May 2024.
As the project entered its final year of implementation after the no-cost extension, a number of project results stemed from the work of the program in terms of enhanced partnership for climate security, knowledge produced, and country-specific resilience grants.
The project managed to advance the climate security agenda in the Arab States by galvanizing political support through the strategic partnership with LAS, which was instrumental in placing human security at the centre stage of Member States debates, and high-level events such as COP27 and COP28. Policy debates were translated into action on the ground thanks to the country resilience grants in Iraq, Jordan, Tunisia, Yemen, the State of Palestine, and Egypt, demonstrating the relevance of integrated approaches to attract climate finance for human security in the region.
For instance, in Iraq, the findings and studies facilitated by resilience grants played a pivotal role in incorporating climate security concerns into the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). This underscores the gravity of climate change's impact on livelihoods, security, and peace within the community. Moreover, it suggests solutions that intertwine water management with food security, biodiversity preservation, and human well-being.
Integrated solutions can deliver scaled up finance for climate-oriented solutions for human security as elaborated in the research conducted by UNEP FI, and in the context of the UNDP led Ministries of Finance for Climate Action initiative, which include lessons learned on leveraging multilateral and bilateral climate finance sources and removing barriers to expand the private sector engagement and investment in climate action to increase. This specifically applies to Tunisia, Iraq, Jordan and the State of Palestine, where UNDP has managed to mobilize climate finance from GEF, Canada, Japan, Germany and the private sector to scale up the results of the country resilience grants, totalling to approximately US$17M, with additional USD 27 M in the pipeline for climate security in Yemen through financial support from GEF and KfW.
The SDG-Climate Facility ensured gender responsiveness throughout the project, promoting the leadership role of women and girls in conservation and restoration efforts to develop gender action plans and gender gap analysis, and mainstream gender equality and womens knowledge in climate-oriented solutions. Lesson learned through the project showcase that climate action would not achieve meaningful results without overcoming gender disparities; for example, through the partnership between AWC, UN Women, UNHCR, and UNDP, new insights were produced on the impact of climate change on women, with a particular focus on displaced women, providing practical recommendations for practitioners on the ground on enhancing gender equality and the protection of vulnerable women in climate action and climate security.
This refined understanding of the implication of gender mainstreaming in climate action materialized in the resilience grants, where the percentage of women benefitting from the project were later translated into recommendations to capture their knowledge on how to adapt to climate change with limited resources and provide recommendations for policymakers to enhance integrated approaches and stakeholder consultations that takes the most vulnerable into considerations with the new revision of the NDCs.
The resilience grants showcased during the reporting year that political and programmatic strategies need to ensure the inclusion, meaningful participation, and empowerment of all relevant actors, including youth, women, and other vulnerable groups such as displaced people to reflect their experience and leverage diverse knowledge. This approach was also mainstreamed into the UN Climate Security Mechanism and UNDPs global initiative Climate Promiseto enhance NDCs and NAPs across the Arab States and beyond.
Some additional results included:
Implementation of the 7 country resilience grants: during the no-cost extension period, the project team accelerated and finalized the implementation of the country grants in Tunisia, Egypt, Yemen, and Iraq. Upon the successful results of the grant in Jordan, the project was able to scale up the grant to include more beneficiaries. Leveraging the implementation of the pilots, UNDP country offices have managed to guarantee the sustainability of the resilience grants by attracting additional funding from multilateral donors, as well as the private and public sectors, by showcasing concrete results and engaging local stakeholders.
Knowledge products: during the no-cost extension, the project finalized and launched several knowledge products at high-level regional events such as the Middle East and North Africa Climate Week 2023 and COP28. The projects knowledge products reached a larger number of people in these events and approximately 37,000 on digital platforms
